lesson.title: Trading the Curve for Its Tangent Line
lesson.summary: Tangent line approximation uses the straight line that best hugs a curve at one point to estimate the function's value nearby, turning the geometric idea of local linearity into a practical calculation tool.
lesson.body:
Local linearity says that a differentiable curve looks like its tangent line under close enough magnification, and tangent approximation, also called linearization, is simply the decision to take that resemblance seriously as a computational shortcut. Instead of evaluating a complicated function f directly at some input near a, you evaluate the much simpler linear function L(x) = f(a) + f'(a)(x - a) instead, trusting that L(x) will be close to f(x) whenever x is close to a, precisely because the two are locally indistinguishable near that point.

The technique is most useful exactly when f(a) and f'(a) are easy to compute but f(x) itself, at some nearby but inconvenient value, is not. A classic case is estimating a square root by hand. Let f(x) be the square root of x, and choose a = 4, since the square root of 4 is the easy, exact value 2. The derivative is f'(x) = 1 / (2 times the square root of x), so f'(4) = 1 / (2 times 2) = 1/4 = 0.25. The linearization is therefore L(x) = 2 + 0.25(x - 4).

Use this to estimate the square root of 4.1, a value with no clean exact form. Plug x = 4.1 into the linearization: L(4.1) = 2 + 0.25 times (4.1 - 4) = 2 + 0.25 times 0.1 = 2 + 0.025 = 2.025. The true value of the square root of 4.1 is approximately 2.02485, found by more precise computation. The tangent line estimate of 2.025 differs from the true value by only about 0.00015, an extremely small error achieved using nothing more than one multiplication and one addition, in place of directly extracting a square root.

The accuracy of this approximation is not accidental, and it is not unlimited either. Because the tangent line only truly matches the curve in the immediate neighborhood of a, the quality of the estimate degrades as x moves farther away from a, exactly as local linearity would predict, since the resemblance between curve and line was only ever a close-up phenomenon. Estimating the square root of 9 using the same tangent line built at a = 4 would give L(9) = 2 + 0.25 times 5 = 3.25, while the true value is exactly 3, an error of 0.25, which is far worse than the error at x = 4.1. The lesson is that tangent approximation is a local tool: reliable very close to the point where the tangent line was built, and increasingly unreliable the farther the target input strays from that point.

This simple linear estimate underlies far more advanced techniques used later in calculus, including differentials and iterative root-finding methods, but its core idea never changes: replace a curve you cannot easily evaluate with the straight line that, thanks to local linearity, behaves almost exactly like the curve does in the immediate vicinity of a known point.

It is also worth noting what tangent approximation quietly assumes: that f is actually differentiable at a in the first place. At a corner, a cusp, or a vertical tangent point, there is no single tangent line to build L(x) from, so the technique simply does not apply there. This is one more reason the earlier classification of non-differentiable points matters beyond its own section: before trusting any linear approximation near a point, it is worth confirming that the point is an ordinary differentiable one, with a genuine finite slope, and not one of the sharper features where local linearity breaks down.
